questions.q: Why does the dependency-layer caching pattern from Lesson 3 matter even more for an AI app's Dockerfile?
options: AI apps never need a requirements.txt file
Packages like torch or transformers are much larger than typical web dependencies, so an uncached reinstall costs minutes, not seconds
AI apps cannot use a base image smaller than 1GB
Caching only works for Flask applications
questions.explain: A full dependency reinstall for a PyTorch-style stack is far more expensive than for a typical web framework, so avoiding unnecessary cache invalidation matters more.

questions.q: What problem does a `.dockerignore` file solve for an AI project specifically?
options: It makes `pip install` run faster
It automatically compresses model weight files
It prevents large, unneeded local files like virtual environments and checkpoints from being sent as part of the build context
It encrypts the Dockerfile
questions.explain: Without it, everything in the project directory — including multi-gigabyte venvs or stray checkpoints — gets uploaded to the Docker daemon on every build.

questions.q: Why must the FastAPI example bind to `0.0.0.0` rather than `127.0.0.1`?
options: 0.0.0.0 is required by the FastAPI framework specifically
127.0.0.1 only works with GPU containers
Binding to 127.0.0.1 would make the build fail entirely
A server bound to 127.0.0.1 only accepts connections from inside the same container, refusing traffic from outside it
questions.explain: 127.0.0.1 (localhost) is only reachable from within the container itself; 0.0.0.0 accepts connections from outside, which `docker run -p` depends on.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what changes about `docker build` and `docker run` themselves when containerizing an AI app instead of a typical web app?
options: Nothing about the commands themselves changes — what changes is what's inside the image
docker run requires a special `--ai` flag
docker build must be run twice for any AI app
A completely different set of commands is required
questions.explain: The build/run loop from Lesson 4 is unchanged; what differs is the content of the image — larger dependencies and a model file.

questions.q: Why is loading the model file once at startup, rather than on every request, the better pattern in this lesson's example?
options: It's required by Docker's build cache
It has no effect on performance either way
Reloading a model file on every request would reload it from disk repeatedly instead of once, wasting time on every call
Docker does not allow a model file to be read more than once
questions.explain: Loading the model once at module level, as the example does, avoids the cost of re-reading the model file from disk on every single prediction request.
